items.descriptionOriginal: You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified. Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging. Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator. Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it? Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out. What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant? On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Photograph: (Plastic Pollution Coalition) Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs. Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026 . After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed. FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies. A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed. How does bromate get into water? Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation , is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount. How much forms depends on four things: how much bromide was in the water to begin with how much ozone is used the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is) how long treatment runs Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. Photograph: (The Hospital of Central Connecticut) Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities. So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching. How much is too much? Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans. That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count. The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested. In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long. Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking. What are PAHs, and how do they get into water? PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment. PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO , one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Photograph: (Image generated by AI) One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk. Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from. What about the plastic bottle? Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got. Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here. What checks are already in place? Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order , packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means: manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration inspections happen once a year centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to: test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection. How does a failed sample end up in court? The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 , sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47): A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report. If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory. If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. Photograph: (Food & Wine) In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process. Should consumers be worried? Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals . But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe. Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

items.descriptionOriginal: When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy. For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat. In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes. A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort. Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived. Why roadside trees matter to orchids Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once. The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala. A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot , recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics. The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support. The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK. More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme. The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. Three sites, different survival outcomes The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region. Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas. Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. Photograph: (tspkumar via iNaturalist) Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray. The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment , while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive. However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%. It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively. What the findings mean for conservation The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%. The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka. This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions. The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site. Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc — Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026 Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants , indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations. However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided. Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed. Sources: 'When Roads Remove Trees, Conservation Must Move Fast: A Rescue Translocation Model for Keralam's Native Epiphytic Orchids' : By Mithun Venugopal , Pradeep N. Sukumaran, Viswambharan Sarasan, Published on 15 October 2026 'Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot' : By Viswambharan Sarasan, Mithun Venugopal, Ratheesh M. items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia What if surgeons could perform a heart bypass without stopping the heart? Two Indian doctors just made it possible! At Medanta Hospital in Gurugram, Dr Nitin Kumar Rajput and Dr Lalit Malik performed a complex heart bypass using five robotic arms controlled through two separate surgeon consoles. The procedure, called Totally Endoscopic Coronary Artery Bypass (TECAB), was performed through tiny incisions without the conventional large chest incision or stopping the heart. A specialised stabiliser held the area being operated on steady while the heart continued beating. No heart-lung machine was needed. This was the world’s first reported dual-console, five-arm robotic beating-heart TECAB procedure. And here’s another reason to celebrate: the robot used was SSi Mantra, developed in India by SS Innovations, founded by cardiac surgeon Dr Sudhir Srivastava. The patient’s recovery has been encouraging. A remarkable step forward for Indian medical innovation and the future of minimally invasive heart surgery! #RoboticSurgery #HeartSurgery #MedicalInnovation #MakeInIndia #IndianInnovation [Robotic heart bypass surgery in India, world’s first beating-heart TECAB, SSi Mantra surgical robot, Indian-mad Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

Για χρόνια, το θέαμα μιας ενυδρίδας που κολυμπά…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare. Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution. Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways. A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge , documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley. Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction. The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline. Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply. The return was first noticed in 2025 According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral. Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile. The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Photograph: (IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin) Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025. Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area. Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley . The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district. The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river. The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs. The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights. However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley. Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health. A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation. More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats. What could threaten their return? The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported. Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals. The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats. Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival. We are into the middle stage of our '13 Weeks of Otters' series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv — International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022 Climate change presents another challenge. Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms , which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley. What conservation efforts need to focus on The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations. This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations. It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters. The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour. The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral. Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley. Sources: 'Re‐Emergence of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra Lutra ) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge' : By Irfan Khursheed Shah, Sohail Ahmad Wagay, Published in October 2026 'Eurasian Otters Make Remarkable Re-Emergence In Kashmir Valley After Decades-Long Absence' : By Eurasia Review, Published on 8 November 2026 'An Overview on Lutra lutra' : By Seyed Parsa Mousavi, Mohammad Mahdi Ramzanipour, and Mohammad Forouhar Vajargah, Published on 15 April 2023 'The Satpura Otter Saga' : By Raza Kazmi, Wildlife Conservation Trust, Published in December 2024

Οι ιστορίες διάσωσης μωρού ελέφαντα σπάνια τελειώνουν τόσο καλά όσο του Zuri. Βρέθηκε εγκλωβισμένος μέσα σε σηπτική δεξαμενή κοντά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal Reading Time: 3 minutes Baby elephant rescue Zuri has thrived for months at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s Nairobi Nursery after nearly drowning in a septic tank in Kenya. Baby elephant rescue stories rarely end as well as Zuri’s. Found trapped inside a septic tank near Voi Safari Lodge in Kenya when she was just days old, the calf has spent the past months recovering at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s nursery in Nairobi. Keepers now describe a confident, food-driven toddler who has already claimed the role of herd princess. Rescuers worked late into the night to free Zuri from the tank, a traumatic ordeal for any elephant calf, let alone one only days old. After a night of stabilization at the Trust’s nearby Voi facility, she was flown to the Nairobi Nursery for round-the-clock care. The Nairobi Nursery is the first stop in a rehabilitation journey that can stretch for more than a decade. Orphaned elephants typically arrive after losing their mothers to poaching, drought, conflict, or accidents like Zuri’s. Keepers assign each calf a dedicated human caregiver who stays close around the clock, standing in for the mother an orphan has lost. Each baby elephant rescue brings its own logistical demands. Calves depend on a specialized milk formula that took decades of trial and error to perfect, since cow’s milk alone proved fatal to earlier generations of rescued elephants. Round-the-clock bottle feeding, veterinary monitoring, and a rotating team of keepers all continue for months or years after a calf first arrives. Within days of arriving, Zuri settled into the nursery herd and quickly displaced an older calf as the group’s most doted-on member. Several older orphans now compete to shepherd her around, with one in particular walking her into her stable each evening for weeks, until Zuri felt ready to go in alone. Keepers describe Zuri as anything but timid. She reportedly bangs on her stable door the moment she hears a wheelbarrow of milk bottles approaching at night, and sprints toward keepers with her trunk raised during the day, visibly displeased if a bottle isn’t ready and waiting. She has even tried stealing bottles from an older herd mate after finishing her own. Despite her boldness, Zuri shows a softer side around the nursery’s newest arrival, a recently rescued calf not yet publicly introduced. Keepers say Zuri doesn’t treat the newcomer as a rival the way she does with some of the older toddlers, a distinction they see as a promising sign of her continued emotional development. Bold enough to bang on her stable door at feeding time and steal milk bottles from herd mates, Zuri also shows a gentler side with the nursery’s newest arrival, a sign keepers read as promising emotional growth in the baby elephant rescue. Photo courtesy of Sheldrick Wildlife Trust . Not every trace of the ordeal has faded. Zuri remains wary of unfamiliar people and some of her own keepers, a caution the Trust attributes to her brush with drowning and the fear she experienced during the traumatic rescue. Recovery from early trauma varies widely between individual elephants, and keepers say patience, gentle care, reassurance, and close observation, rather than a fixed timeline, guide each calf’s progress. Over time, they hope Zuri will continue building confidence and feel increasingly secure in her new environment. Zuri’s progress reflects decades of institutional experience behind this kind of baby elephant rescue work. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has run its elephant rescue and rehabilitation program since the 1970s, hand-raising hundreds of orphans and successfully returning most to wild herds in Tsavo. Public support directly funds this kind of work. Individual donors can foster a specific orphan, supporting a program that covers keeper salaries, milk formula, and veterinary costs for calves like Zuri. That funding model has let the Trust scale its operations even as new rescue calls keep coming in from across Kenya. Around three years old, Zuri will eventually graduate from the nursery to one of the Trust’s reintegration units in Tsavo, following the same path generations of orphans before her took. For now, her days are filled with milk, mischief, and the attention of a devoted entourage of nannies. For a calf whose baby elephant rescue began three months ago with a near-drowning in a septic tank, that counts as a very good life. The post Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. “As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. “Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning, environment and health initiative at ISGlobal, a public health research institute based in Barcelona. “Many cities are now following their direction: It reduces air pollution, noise, and livability improves.” Over the course of the 20th century, the city came to be dominated by vehicles. By the late 1990s, an average of 80,000 cars drove through Pontevedra every day — astonishingly, according to the municipality, three times more than through Madrid and five times more than London. Many of these vehicles weren’t even heading for the city, but rather transiting to other destinations such as beach towns on the coast. Those that did stay would turn the city’s charming historic squares into parking lots. Pontevedra before it was redesigned for pedestrians. Credit: Council of Pontevedra This came at a cost. Pontevedra’s epoch of cars dirtied the air, led to the deaths of pedestrians and seized centuries-old public spaces from residents. “The city was loud, disagreeable, unlivable,” says Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra, from the desk of his city hall office. “All the roads were filled with cars. The city was like a huge, permanent traffic jam.” Fernández Lores, a doctor by trade, decided enough was enough. In 1999, he campaigned to reclaim Pontevedra’s streets. The population agreed and elected him. Yet the urban transformation was not overnight. It has been carried out gradually. Fernández Lores began with a major effort to keep unnecessary cars out of the historic city center, removing significant amounts of on-street parking and only allowing essential vehicles to enter. Within one month in office, he had pedestrianized 300,000 square meters of the city center. In other parts of the city, he narrowed roads and widened sidewalks, introduced 30 kilometer per hour speed limits citywide, down from 50 kilometers per hour, and began installing traffic-calming measures like raised pedestrian crosswalks as well as almost 300 speed bumps. To take one example, the central Benito Corbel Street once had four lanes of traffic. In 2000, that was reduced to two lanes with widened sidewalks and trees. By 2014, it became a single-track road with only service vehicles able to enter, and even then for a limited time. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The mayor, who passed a Traffic and Mobility Plan for Pontevedra in 2011 formalizing and defining his pedestrian-first approach, also developed infrastructure to make it easier to ditch cars. The city now has roughly 4,500 private underground parking spaces and about 3,500 free “park and ride” spaces, all within a short walking distance from the center. Traffic lights were replaced by roundabouts to facilitate the flow of the remaining vehicles. In some central areas, the speed limit was lowered to just 10 kilometers per hour. Trees, green spaces and street lighting were also added to improve livability. But despite its reputation, Pontevedra is not completely car-free — it allows certain vehicles on its streets within reason. “It’s not a city without cars,” says Fernández Lores. “But we only let the ones that really need to come here in.” Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra. Credit: Peter Yeung Residents can drive to garaged parking spots in the city. People with disabilities are free to drive in Pontevedra as long as they have a permit. And vehicles used for emergencies and public services such as garbage and water trucks and ambulances are permitted 24/7. Home deliveries, house moving and loading and unloading by businesses are allowed, but only during certain hours. And indeed, taxi drivers like Barbosa may enter certain zones if they have a client or booking. When necessary, police can issue fines of several hundred euros, ensuring these limits are respected. “I think it was very smart, the decisions they made,” says Mirian Calvo , a researcher and expert in urban design from Pontevedra. “And this philosophy, of mixed-traffic, prioritizing soft mobility, has been applied over 30 years, more or less.” The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Car trips in the city center have fallen by 97 percent, according to official municipal figures. The air is markedly cleaner, with CO2 emissions dropping by about 70 percent. And the streets are much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011, whereas between 1996 and 2006, 30 people died in traffic accidents. (Pontevedra has won European road safety awards in the process.) The streets of Pontevedra have gotten much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011. Credit: Pilar Picas / Shutterstock In fact, about 90 percent of all journeys in the city center are by foot, with road safety so high that 80 percent of kids aged 6 to 12 walk without their parents to school each morning. Many local business owners have signed up to be supervisors if the children need help for any reason. For all the talk of the climate and safety benefits that come with limiting vehicle traffic and designing pedestrian-first urban spaces, however, there has been a surprising further advantage: Pontevedra is thriving economically. While in the 1990s, retail activity was drifting towards the suburbs, the decision to prioritize a compact, walkable city with a high quality of life, has changed the picture drastically. The mayor, for his part, has rejected proposals to build malls on the urban periphery, protecting the pedestrian-oriented urban core. “We don’t want huge malls, we want small, independent businesses,” says Fernández Lores. Pontevedra is now the fastest-growing city in the region of Galicia and in recent years has attracted 15,000 new inhabitants, mostly young families from elsewhere in northwest Spain. It also generates more jobs per capita than any other city in the region. The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Credit: Peter Yeung “It’s a very convenient city now,” says Calvo. “It’s a very nice city to live in and people can see that.” Most locals are effusive in their praise. Esther Louzao, 68, says that her home near Plaza Pelegrina was once surrounded by cars, but not anymore. She has even stopped driving to work, instead opting to go by bus. But she keeps her car for beach days. “I like it a lot, it’s easier to walk,” says Louzao, fittingly waiting at a bus stop. Pacing down the street with a stroller, Anna, a 39-year-old with a toddler son who lives four kilometers out of town, agrees. “It’s better, much safer, it’s pleasant,” she explains. “Even if sometimes my journeys take a bit longer.” Yet not all residents are entirely convinced by the policy. Manuel, who has been living in Pontevedra for 40 years, believes the transformation has been overstated. He owns three cars: one for the city, one for going to the beach and a third for sport driving. “Yes, the city is a lot different to how it was before,” says Manuel. “But it’s not as perfect as it seems. Some of us still need cars.” In Spain, all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants are now required have a low emission zone, like this one in Santander. Credit: Scharfsinn / Shutterstock Calvo agrees, noting that Pontevedra’s public transit network is lacking, which means that elderly people suffer and that cars must be taken to the coastal beaches. A system like Rome’s fleet of electric minibuses in the historic center could be implemented, she says. And although the results of Pontevedra’s policy are hard to deny, Calvo, who is also a lecturer in participatory architecture, argues that the system could have been even more effective and popular if residents had been more involved in the process. In the 2000s, she says, there was significant opposition to the project, even if that has now disappeared due to the clearly positive impact. “I don’t think there has been serious public engagement,” she says. “There are more things that could be done to make it more participatory.” Nieuwenhuijsen, however, commends Pontevedra’s less confrontational approach, which presented the restriction of cars as about livability. “I think everyone would prefer places with less noise and less pollution,” he says. “It shouldn’t be about the war on cars, presented as punishing someone.” In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free. Credit: OlgaVysh / Shutterstock In any case, cities across the world are following in Pontevedra’s pioneering footsteps. In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free by removing on-street parking spaces and restricting access. Freiburg, Germany, has similarly transformed the district of Vauban into a car-free zone, banning on-street parking and introducing vehicle speed limits at walking pace on residential streets. And in 2022, the Spanish government approved a royal decree requiring all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants to have a low emission zone, and recommending the use of traffic-restricted areas like that of Pontevedra. Yet not every place can easily replicate Pontevedra’s success. Professor Nieuwenhuijsen admits the transformation of North American cities could be more challenging given their size and lack of density. “U.S. cities were built around the car,” he says. “You get a lot of sprawl. European cities are different, many were designed for walking and horse carriages.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Likewise, transforming larger cities will not be as easy. Redesigning urban areas could be slowed or halted by infrastructure such as underground piping, adds Nieuwenhuijsen, and the investment required could prove prohibitive. Barcelona’s Superblocks cost as little as €500,000 but as much as €10 million per unit in some cases. But Fernández Lores, who is planning to run for an eighth term in 2027, believes that bigger cities could begin shifting away from cars and towards pedestrians by focusing on districts rather than entire cities. A case in point: In 2023, Culdesac Tempe, Arizona, became the first purpose-built, entirely car-free residential neighborhood in the U.S. “Cities work without cars,” he says. “But each city must find its own way.” The post The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Two people in a waiting area at an animal hospital shared a love for their pets. One brought her dog; the other brought his cat. That connection seemed to bond them for a few hours while one waited for care for her dog, and another waited to say goodbye to his cat. During those hours, there were few words, but several tender acts of care. Though they never even learned one another’s names, a common love, and a few caring acts connected them in an exchange of humanity that will endure. “If I could see him now, all this time later, I would tell him that I’m still thinking of him.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands Reading Time: 3 minutes Genomes from 64 gentoo penguins show the familiar bird is really four species, including the southeastern gentoo, a new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. New penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands? It is rare news in the penguin world. Yet the southeastern gentoo penguin is the first living penguin species named in more than a century. The Kerguelen Islands are a remote, windswept French territory in the southern Indian Ocean. Gentoo penguins have nested there for thousands of years. Until now, no one realized the local birds were their own species. Gentoos are easy to spot. They have a white patch above each eye and a bright orange bill. They are also among the fastest-swimming penguins. For more than a century, scientists treated all gentoos as one widespread species. Some proposed as many as six subspecies, but experts never agreed. A new genetic study now settles the debate. Communications Biology published the study in September 2026. Daly Noll, a graduate student at the University of Chile, led the genetic analysis. Senior authors came from Andrés Bello National University in Chile and the University of California, Berkeley. The team sequenced the full genomes of 64 penguins from 10 breeding colonies. Those colonies span almost the entire gentoo range. The researchers also compared body size, calls, diets, and breeding schedules. Scientists from about a dozen countries helped identify the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. Contributors came from Australia, South Africa, France, Brazil, and beyond. The data revealed four distinct species. The northern gentoo lives on the Falkland Islands and near South America. The eastern gentoo breeds on Crozet, Marion, and Macquarie islands. The southern gentoo occupies the Antarctic Peninsula, coastal Antarctica, and South Georgia. The fourth is the southeastern gentoo ( Pygoscelis kerguelensis ). It lives on the Kerguelen Islands and probably on nearby Heard Island too. Biologists call the southeastern gentoo a cryptic species. It looks almost identical to its relatives, and its differences lie mainly in its genes. Its body size and calls also differ subtly. This new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands has a relatively small population. That makes accurate classification especially important for its protection. The four species began to split between 300,000 and 500,000 years ago. Island isolation played a major role. The Antarctic Polar Front, an ocean boundary where water temperature and salinity change sharply, also played a role. Island isolation and the Antarctic Polar Front helped drive the evolution of four distinct species over hundreds of thousands of years. Photo by Antoine Lamielle on Wikimedia Commons. Gentoos also tend to return to the same colonies year after year. Over time, this loyalty to home kept populations apart. Each group then adapted to its own conditions. A flexible diet helped too. Gentoos eat fish, krill, squid, and cuttlefish, so each population could thrive on whatever its local waters offered. The genomes show those adaptations clearly. Southern gentoos carry genes for heat production and fat storage, while eastern gentoos carry genes for diving. Northern gentoos carry genes linked to digestion and heart function. Dr. Jane Younger of the University of Tasmania first proposed the split in a 2020 paper. Her team later examined museum specimens and found consistent physical differences between regions. She says the new study provides in-depth evidence to support that claim. Why does this matter beyond the name? Treating gentoos as one species produced an overall positive trend. That average hid serious declines in some regions. Southern gentoos on the Antarctic Peninsula are thriving and spreading south. In the Falklands, avian influenza has hit northern gentoos hard in recent years. Populations on Macquarie Island are declining. Climate change raises the stakes for each species. Under a moderate warming scenario, sub-Antarctic gentoos could lose suitable habitat on all their current islands by 2050. Few nearby islands offer alternatives. Antarctic gentoos may fare better and could even expand their range. Emperor, Adélie, and chinstrap penguins, however, are expected to decline as sea ice shrinks and krill supplies change. Other threats include warming seas, introduced rats and dogs, competition with fisheries, and capture in fishing gear. Recognizing each species allows conservation plans to match the threats each one faces. Researchers are already taking next steps. Senior author Juliana Vianna is studying penguin genomes for traits linked to surviving avian influenza. The team has also asked taxonomic authorities to review the split formally. Conservation bodies will need to assess each species separately. That work will determine how much protection the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands receives. A bird seen in countless photos and documentaries turned out to hold hidden diversity . Careful genetic work revealed it. The new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands shows how much remains to be learned about familiar wildlife. The post Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A classroom fan spins above a group of children bent over their notebooks. As the teacher moves between desks and lessons continue, the fan keeps the air circulating. But in a city like Delhi, where pollution often makes its way indoors, circulating air does not necessarily mean breathing clean air. Project Vayu's balloon-shaped filter fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping capture fine particulate matter from classroom air. For thousands of children studying in schools that cannot afford expensive air purifiers, this is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day inside classrooms, often with little protection from fine particulate matter suspended in the air. Two Delhi teenagers, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle, decided to look at this problem differently. Instead of asking schools to invest in expensive purification systems, they wondered if the fans already fitted in classrooms could be made to do more. Their idea took shape as Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed an affordable filter that fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping turn them into air purifiers. At approximately Rs 140 per filter, the innovation offers schools a way to tackle indoor air pollution without having to invest in entirely new equipment. "Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo say. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection." What if a classroom fan could also clean the air? Rather than building a new appliance from scratch, Krish and Samarth decided to work with the infrastructure schools already had. The biggest technical challenge was developing a filter that could trap fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, without restricting the airflow of an ordinary fan. "We experimented with different designs before arriving at our balloon-shaped filter, made from electret media with electrostatically charged fibres," they explain. The filter uses electrostatically charged fibres that attract and capture tiny airborne particles. It fits over an existing table or wall fan with the help of an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates the filter into a balloon-like shape, increasing its surface area for filtration. There is no need for additional motors, electrical modifications or specialised installation. The filter can be fitted in under a minute, without tools. To develop and test the technology , the teenagers approached Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. They initially emailed the company's India team with their idea and were surprised by its willingness to support them. The company provided filtration media free of cost and collaborated with the team on research and development. Priced at approximately Rs 140, the filter offers under-resourced schools an affordable alternative to expensive air purification systems. "The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it. By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure," they say. This support has helped keep the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter. What difference can a Rs 140 filter make? For the young innovators , developing an affordable product was only half the task. They also needed to establish whether it could make a measurable difference to indoor air quality. According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research and development with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results. In a closed room measuring approximately 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly dropped from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour of using the filter, a reduction of over 90%. The results, however, depend on the room's size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 levels over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use. There is also a visible reminder of the particles being trapped. "One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use. It's a visible reminder of just how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms," they say. From 295 classrooms to thousands of students Getting schools to trust an unfamiliar technology developed by high school students was not easy. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and around 8,000 students. It has since reached approximately 20,000 students across more than 10 schools. Initially, many institutions were understandably hesitant. Demonstrations and explanations of the testing behind the filters, however, helped the team build confidence. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and approximately 8,000 students. The initiative has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics. Their work has not been without challenges. Identifying schools, securing permissions and navigating institutional processes have often slowed installations. "Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging. A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals," they say. The effort has also brought recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his work with Project Vayu. For him, the recognition belongs to everyone who helped build the initiative, including Samarth and their collaborators. "Project Vayu has taught me that innovation doesn't always require inventing something entirely new. Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible," Samarth adds. What's next for Project Vayu? The duo now hopes to expand Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and eventually other parts of India. They are keen to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help take the filters to children who need them. Their ambition is rooted in a simple belief: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend. For Krish and Samarth, the idea was never just about making a fan work differently. It was about looking at something already available in classrooms and asking how it could serve children better. And sometimes, making a difference does not require an entirely new machine. It begins with finding a new purpose for something that is already there. items.descriptionOriginal: A handful of seeds can carry generations of farming knowledge. In Karnataka's Dharwad district, a group of women has been collecting, preserving, and sharing these seeds, helping farmers continue cultivating indigenous crops suited to the region's rainfed conditions. On November 12, 2026, the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group (SHG) from Teertha village in Kundgol taluk received the Plant Genome Saviour Community Award, along with a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh, a citation, and a memento. The recognition acknowledges the collective's efforts to conserve more than 250 indigenous seed varieties and revive traditional millet-based mixed cropping systems across 30 villages in Dharwad's rainfed farming areas. The initiative began in 2018, when farmer Bibijaan Maulasaab Halemani brought together 14 other women to establish the collective. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Photograph: (The Hindu) According to Bibijaan, her interest in seed conservation came from her father, who also preserved seeds. Speaking to The New Indian Express in a report published on November 5, 2026, she said, "My father used to conserve seeds, and I too developed an interest and took to seed conservation." She established the SHG and its seed bank in 2018, with the aim of making good-quality indigenous seeds accessible to farmers and encouraging traditional crop cultivation. A seed bank with more than 250 varieties The group's community seed bank preserves a wide range of indigenous crops, including: - Jawari (sorghum) - 70 varieties of finger millet - 25 varieties of little millet - Two varieties of browntop millet - 10 varieties of foxtail millet - 25 varieties of horse gram - 10 varieties of chickpea - 25 varieties of paddy - Three varieties of green gram - Around a dozen oilseed varieties - Several varieties of vegetables These varieties form part of the region's traditional agricultural diversity. The indigenous millet varieties, in particular, are adapted to local agro-climatic conditions and can withstand variations in weather. The collective has also worked to revive millet-based mixed cropping, in which farmers cultivate multiple crops together rather than depending on a single crop. According to the United Nations Development Programme's Equator Initiative, the group now supports more than 5,000 farmers across 30 villages. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Beyond seed conservation, the collective has expanded into agricultural processing and livelihood activities. It operates a solar-powered millet processing unit, which helps women produce value-added millet products. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Recognition for community-led seed conservation The national award is not the group's first recognition for its work. In August 2025, the United Nations Development Programme announced Bibifathima Swa Sahaya Sangha as one of the 10 winners of the Equator Prize 2025. The award recognised community-led initiatives working on nature-based solutions under the theme 'Nature for Climate Action', with a focus on women's and young people's leadership. According to the UNDP's August 20, 2025 announcement, the collective received recognition for its work combining traditional agricultural knowledge, seed conservation, renewable energy and climate-resilient farming. Each winning initiative was awarded $10,000. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Photograph: (National Commission for Women/Facebook) For the women of Dharwad, their work continues to centre on collecting indigenous seeds, keeping traditional crop varieties in cultivation and helping farming communities access planting material suited to their local conditions. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular feeling that comes with lifting the lid off the holiday storage bin. The tangle of lights, the ornament with the chipped corner, the little ceramic village you’ve set up on the same shelf for as long as you can remember. It’s comforting, and there’s a reason traditions stick around. But somewhere around the third box, the comfort can start to tip into a sort of déjà vu, and you might catch yourself wondering whether it’s time to start over. Before you head to the store, though, try a different idea. The holiday decorations you already own can look surprisingly different with a little rearranging, a few things from outside, and a willingness to break your own habits. Here are six ways to do it, whether you’re decking the halls for Thanksgiving , Christmas, Hanukkah or all of the above. Rethinking where holiday decorations go Give every piece a new home Most of us decorate on autopilot. The wreath goes on the same hook, the nativity scene lands on the same bookshelf, and the whole house ends up looking exactly like it did last year, because it is exactly like last year. This time, pause before you put anything down. Hold each piece and ask where else it could live. That nativity scene might feel brand new on the entryway table, where it’s the first thing people see. If you’re stuck, give yourself a rule: everything that usually goes upstairs goes downstairs this year, and vice versa. Choose one theme and edit to fit it Instead of pulling out every decoration you own, pick a theme and use only what matches. It can be as simple as one color, like all greens, or one motif, like snowflakes or anything that sparkles. Leaving some favorites in the box for a year can make them feel special again when they come back out, and the pieces you do use will look more intentional together. Bringing in natural and handmade touches Decorate with what’s growing outside Your backyard or a neighborhood walk can fill in a lot of gaps at no cost. A handful of pinecones lined along the mantel, or a few bare branches standing tall in a big vase on the kitchen island, adds texture and makes the familiar pieces around them look fresher. Dried citrus is another easy one. Slice oranges or grapefruit thin, dry them in a low oven until they turn translucent, and string them into a garland. Any extra slices make a lovely garnish for a winter drink. Add something your family made Handmade decorations carry a warmth store-bought ones can’t match. You could decide that this is the year the tree only gets ornaments made at the kitchen table, or have everyone in the house paint their own candle for the menorah. The pieces don’t need to be perfect. The slightly lopsided ones tend to become the favorites. Small changes to familiar holiday decor Trade your lights around String lights are easy to move, so let them wander. Bring the indoor lights outside and the outdoor ones in, or take the strand that usually wraps the tree and frame a doorway with it instead. Before anything goes outside, check that it’s rated for outdoor use, since indoor lights left out in the weather can become a fire hazard. Paint, mix and remake If you’re truly tired of a piece, change how it looks. Spray paint a set of old ornaments in a new color, hand-paint plain candles, or combine figures from two or three mismatched nativity sets into one scene. Experimenting is low-risk here. If you end up disliking the result, you were already ready to retire it, and if you love it, you’ve got something that feels new without buying a single thing, which might be the nicest kind of holiday surprise there is. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone. The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 , passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law. How the abortion pardons work Records deleted, or treated as deleted The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased. Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls , said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said. What remains illegal The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges. Ending a Victorian law’s reach Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along. Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said. It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was. Reactions to the pardons Providers and advocates Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said. Opponents of decriminalization Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.” For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows. items.descriptionOriginal: An evocative shot of a waterfall of fog spilling into the sea in Mallorca, Spain, took the top honor in the Royal Meteorological Society’s 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition. Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the image during dawn’s first light, the rising sun illuminating the mist. “There’s a fabulous sense of flow in this image,” competition judge Angela Nicholson said in a statement. “The clouds are transformed into a river flowing over the cliffs. Francisco’s choice of exposure has captured the movement of the clouds perfectly below a beautiful sky with subtle color transitions.” Now in its second decade, the competition highlights the beauty and power of weather while raising awareness of the environmental issues that threaten life on Earth — things like heat, fires, and floods. Thirty images were shortlisted from a pool of over 5,500 taken in 13 countries. In addition to Rodríguez’s shot, eight photos were recognized as winners or runners-up across four categories: public vote, mobile, climate, and main. “These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, per SWNS, adding: “Crucially, many of these images also deliver a powerful and urgent message about the global impact of climate change on environments ranging from parched agricultural land to melting ice caps.” The annual competition is free to enter and open to photographers of all ages and abilities, with judges looking for images that combine skill, meteorological observation, and storytelling. Take a look at the other winners and runners-up, with captions courtesy of contest organizers. Public Vote | Winner “Misty Sunrise Over the Long Coc Tea Hills” by Mahmudul Hasan Mahmudul Hasan/RMetS/SWNS “Captured in the delicate light of dawn, this breathtaking photo reveals the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.” Mobile Category | Winner “A Winter Morning” by Aung Soe Min Aung Soe MinRMetS/SWNS “A calm winter morning reveals Kuthodaw Pagoda rising through the mist and fog. Aung Soe Min captured the sun rays filtering across the landscape, creating a beautiful sunrise that captures the warmth of the weather and the peaceful serenity of this sacred site in Myanmar.” Climate Award | Winner “Fire” by Erfan Samanfar Erfan Samanfar/RMetS/SWNS “From Marvdasht, Iran, in October 2025, Erfan Samanfar captured a striking image of a farmer attempting to protect their land as fire spreads across the landscape.” Main Category | Runner-Up “Sunrise and Morning Glow” by Weilu Chen Weilu ChenRMetS/SWNS “As the sun rose over the Hong Kong Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the morning sky was transformed into a spectacular display of golden light.” Public Vote | Runner-Up “Triple Strike NYC” by Dan Martland Dan Martland/RMetS/SWNS “Talk about being in the right place at the right time. From Bayonne, New Jersey, Dan Martland captured this spectacular scene overlooking the New York City skyline, as three lightning strikes lit the sky above the city.” Mobile Category | Runner-Up “A Rainbow Over Loch Duck” by Anthony Bird Anthony BirdRMetS/SWNS “Framed by the rolling hills and water below, a magnificent rainbow arches across the landscape of Loch Duck, Scotland. The scene caught Anthony Bird’s eye so quickly that there was barely time to think, as he simply had to ‘run outside the Airbnb’ to capture it.” Climate Award | Runner-Up “Castles in the Wind” by Andres Miraglia Andres Miraglia/RMetS/SWNS “As an iceberg drifted away from the glacier that released it in Antarctica’s Paradise Harbour, Andres Miraglia captured the moment against a pristine sunset.” Main Category | Third Place “A Supercell in the Sandhills of Nebraska” by Laura Hedien Laura Hedien/RMetS/SWNS “While out storm chasing in the Nebraska sandhills, ‘Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night,’ explains Laura Hedien.” This article was originally written by Dean Murray for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets .

items.descriptionOriginal: In Assam’s Hatikhuli village, elephants were once feared and chased as they moved through farms, creating conflict between people and wildlife. But a simple idea changed the story: feed, don’t fight. Led by 90-year-old conservationist Pradip Kumar Bhuyan, Binod Dulu Bora, and the local community, Hatikhuli began finding ways for humans and elephants to coexist. Villagers planted food for elephants, mapped their migration routes, and worked to create safer corridors for these gentle giants. Today, over 300 elephants pass through Hatikhuli every year, offering a powerful example of what can happen when communities choose understanding over conflict. This is more than an inspiring conservation story. It’s a reminder that protecting wildlife doesn't always mean keeping humans and animals apart. Sometimes, it means learning how to share the same landscape. items.descriptionOriginal: In the mountain villages of Uttarakhand's Tehri Garhwal district, the amount of drinking water available to families can change dramatically with the seasons. Many households depend on natural springs fed by rainfall and water stored underground. As summer approaches and these springs begin to lose their flow, families are left managing increasingly limited supplies. For residents of Unchaun village in the Kirtinagar block, seasonal water shortages have been a concern. And their experience is shared by several other villages in the region. A 2023–24 annual report by Himmotthan Society documents a similar challenge in Sabli village, also in Tehri Garhwal. A survey conducted in June 2022 found that all 52 households depended on a local spring for drinking water during summer because piped supplies were either unreliable or unavailable. The spring's flow dropped from 30 litres per minute during the monsoon to just five litres per minute in May and June. Over four summer months, the village faced an estimated water deficit of 14 lakh litres. These figures offer a glimpse into how difficult the dry months can be for communities that depend on mountain springs. Now, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Roorkee have developed a new spring in Unchaun, using scientific research to locate and bring underground water to the surface. According to a Ministry of Education announcement on 2 November 2026, the intervention has increased daily drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more during the lean season. The interesting part is how the researchers identified where this water could be found. Where does a Himalayan spring get its water? The intervention is part of IIT Roorkee's project, Rejuvenation of Drying Springs in Takoli Gad Catchment of Tehri District, Uttarakhand . Led by Professor Abhayanand Singh Maurya from the Department of Earth Sciences, the project draws on two studies examining how Himalayan springs are replenished and how water moves through underground rock formations. The research was conducted in the Takoli Gad watershed, a 143-square-kilometre area in the Lesser Himalayas, within the Alaknanda River basin. The first study, published in the Hydrological Sciences Journal in October 2026, examined where spring water comes from and how it travels underground. Researchers studied rainfall patterns and used measurements of different forms of hydrogen and oxygen, including radioactive tritium, to trace the movement and replenishment of groundwater. Their findings revealed just how important the monsoon is for sustaining Himalayan springs. Approximately 82% of spring-water recharge in the studied watershed comes from monsoon rainfall. Winter precipitation contributes around 10%, while pre-monsoon rainfall accounts for the remaining 8%. In simpler terms, much of the water that eventually emerges from these springs enters the ground during the rainy season. Some of it remains stored underground, helping sustain water sources even months after the monsoon has ended. The researchers also examined how long water stays underground before emerging through springs. A second study, published in Applied Geochemistry in 2026, looked at how the rocks beneath the hills influence the chemical composition of spring water. It found that interactions between water and carbonate rocks play an important role, alongside seasonal rainfall, soil carbon dioxide and human activities. Together, these studies helped researchers understand how springs are replenished, what influences their water quality and where groundwater might be available. IIT Roorkee Research Doubles Water Availability in a Himalayan Village During Lean Season Turning scientific research into tangible impact, IIT Roorkee has developed a new spring in Unchaun village, Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, increasing lean-season drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more per day. Led by Prof. Abhayanand Singh Maurya, Department of Earth Sciences, the initiative combines scientific understanding of spring-recharge dynamics, groundwater processes and geophysical investigations with targeted recharge interventions to address seasonal water scarcity. Supported by Namami Gange, National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, the project demonstrates the potential of research-driven solutions to strengthen rural water security. Building on two research studies published in Hydrological Sciences Journal and Applied Geochemistry, the initiative highlights how scientific insights can translate into effective, locally relevant interventions for Himalayan communities. With Prof. K. K. Pant, Director, IIT Roorkee, emphasising research with societal impact, this effort reinforces the Institute's commitment to advancing sustainable solutions for critical environmental and water challenges. #IITRoorkee #WaterSecurity #HimalayanWater #NamamiGange #SpringRejuvenation #GroundwaterRecharge #ResearchForImpact #SustainableDevelopment @iitroorkee @Director_IITR @cleanganganmcg @DoWRRDGR_MoJS — IIT Roorkee (@iitroorkee) November 2, 2026 How the team brought underground water to the surface The researchers began by studying the rock formations beneath the hillside to identify areas capable of holding and carrying groundwater. Once they located promising water-bearing layers, they estimated their depth and extent. The team then designed trenches along the uphill slope. These trenches help slow rainwater flowing downhill, allowing more of it to seep into the soil and replenish underground water reserves. At a suitable water-bearing layer, the researchers created a controlled opening that allowed groundwater to emerge at the surface. This resulted in a new spring near the road leading to Chandrabadni Temple. The reported result is an increase of at least 500 litres of drinking water available daily during the lean season, a potentially important improvement for households that depend on local sources. Springs are among the most important sources of freshwater for communities across the Indian Himalayan region. Photograph: (Representational image-Jeremy Graham / Alamy) Could this help other Himalayan villages? Across the Himalayas, springs are an important source of drinking water, particularly in remote villages where other supplies can be unreliable. The Unchaun project offers one way of addressing seasonal shortages: studying how water moves beneath a particular hillside before deciding where to intervene. As Professor Maurya explained in the Ministry of Education release, "Understanding the source, movement and seasonal behaviour of spring water is essential to addressing water scarcity." The project has shown promising early results, but its long-term success will depend on whether the new spring continues to provide water through changing seasons. Researchers will need to monitor its flow and water quality over time. For now, the intervention offers a potentially useful approach for other Himalayan villages facing similar shortages, while showing how research into something as familiar as rainwater can help address everyday water needs.
