items.descriptionOriginal: By the time the amla ripened at her father's farm in Iduvai, Tamil Nadu, there was more fruit than the family could consume or sell fresh. Around 25 trees were bearing heavily, and the harvest would not wait for buyers. For Kalaiselvi, a former software professional who had spent nearly a decade working in the United States, the surplus presented a question: Could the fruit be preserved and sold long after its season had passed? That question led to Aruvi Eco Organics, which now makes more than 25 products, from amla jaggery candy and dried fruit to herbal teas and leaf powders. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. The venture also supports a six-member core team. "My father laid the foundation for our venture through his commitment to organic farming. My contribution has been to build on that legacy by trying out how we can process the produce, reduce avoidable losses, and make natural food products available to more people," she tells The Better India . A return to her father's farm Kalaiselvi grew up in an agricultural family in Iduvai. In 1999, her father, Subramaniam, began developing their ancestral land into what the family called Aruvi Farm, growing amla, sapota, mango and guava without chemical pesticides. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. She remembers planting seeds during childhood summer holidays at her aunt's house. Her parents encouraged their daughters to study while keeping a connection to the land, but her own ambitions took her towards computers. After studying computer science and engineering at Kongu Engineering College, she worked in Chennai before moving to the US in 2006 to join her husband. Her IT career included stints at AT&T, Frontier Communications, Verizon and Highmark in Pittsburgh, where she worked as an application developer. In March 2015, the couple returned to India with their two young children. Her father-in-law was facing serious health issues, and they wanted to be closer to their parents and raise their children here. They settled in Chennai, where Kalaiselvi spent time helping the children adjust, then worked in recruitment and scientific publishing. She also started Kana Bags, an initiative making cloth bags as alternatives to plastic ones. When the pandemic disrupted that venture in 2020, with the children's classes moving online, the family began spending more time on the farm in Iduvai. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. "I got a closer understanding of the effort behind cultivation and the challenges that come with storing and managing the harvest," she recalls. The amla crop was particularly abundant. Even with buyers, fresh fruit had a limited window in which it could be sold. "Instead of looking at the surplus just as produce that could not be sold in time, I started seeing it as an opportunity to create value-added products," she says. From a dryer in the living room to a food business Her father showed her a newspaper article on value addition, and she joined an online session offered by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further. He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, and electrical repairs. She began experimenting with drying amla and sapota, initially using a coir-tray dryer that cost about Rs 28,000. She installed it in her Chennai living room; her father sent fruit from the farm by overnight parcel twice a week. The early batches taught her that turning fruit into a product was more complicated than finding a recipe. She sought training at the ICAR-Krishi Vigyan Kendra in Tirupur, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore and the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. Guidance from a food technologist at the Krishi Vigyan Kendra also helped her understand which ideas could be made consistently and sold commercially. "A recipe may work once, but achieving the same taste, texture, and quality consistently across batches is a completely different challenge," she says. "I had to experiment repeatedly, understand how ingredients behave during processing, and learn how factors such as drying, moisture, and storage affect the final product." Training introduced her to around 25 possible products. Rather than produce everything, she and her father chose ideas that suited what grew on the farm and their preference for avoiding artificial colours, flavours and synthetic preservatives. In 2021, the family also tested selling sapota and mango directly to consumers . Their first order was for sapota, but the pilot reinforced how difficult it could be to find buyers before fruit spoiled. By April 2022, the family had moved permanently to Iduvai. Working alongside Subramaniam, Kalaiselvi made the experiments more systematic, and Aruvi began commercial sales towards the end of that year. A June 2023 video about her journey on the agricultural YouTube channel Tamizhan Agri helped introduce the products to a wider audience. What goes into making 25+ natural food products Aruvi's catalogue has grown to more than 25 products, including over a dozen made with amla. Alongside jaggery-sweetened amla candy are dried mango and sapota, moringa and curry leaf powders, herbal infusions and products made from jamun seeds. "I never set out to build a large product line. Each new addition came from identifying an opportunity to make better use of what we grew and finding ways to meet customer needs," Kalaiselvi says. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. The choices extend to packaging. Aruvi uses cotton bags for its herbal dip teas instead of nylon mesh. Produce is harvested, sorted and cleaned, with damaged portions removed. Depending on the product, the team cuts or deseeds fruit before drying or further processing. The team checks each batch for appearance, texture, aroma and moisture, then packages and stores it carefully. Samples are sent to a NABL-accredited laboratory at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore for nutritional and quality assessment. Working without synthetic preservatives makes consistent processing and storage especially important. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. For Kalaiselvi, this is where her previous career has proved useful. The discipline of software development, she says, helped her approach new recipes through testing, documentation and problem-solving, even as she learnt the practicalities of working with seasonal crops. The people behind every packet As orders grew, Aruvi's work created roles beyond the family. Six people now make up its core team across farming, processing, packaging and operations. For some, the change has meant a dependable income; for others, a chance to use or develop new skills. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. A single mother raising two children, she had previously worked in tailoring and papad-making units. She began by collecting leaves and fruit, then learnt food processing from Kalaiselvi. Today she helps maintain the workspace, stitches cotton tea bags and operates the amla-deseeding machine. "I did not have much knowledge of food processing or how farm produce could be turned into different products," she says. "At Aruvi Eco, I got the opportunity to learn new skills under the guidance of Kalaiselvi ma'am." Earning Rs 5,000 a week has made a difference at home. Her daughter is in college and her teenage son is studying for a diploma. Where she once sometimes turned to relatives for help with education expenses, she says she can now meet more of those costs herself. "Today, I feel proud that I can earn and take care of many of my family's needs myself," she says. "Apart from being my only source of income, this job is an opportunity to build a better future for my children." Ramar and his wife Uma joined in March 2026. They had moved to Tirupur in search of work and were employed at a stitching unit when they saw an advertisement for jobs at Aruvi. Ramar has a degree in agriculture and now handles planting, watering, pruning and tree care under Subramaniam's guidance. Uma works with fruit and flowers in processing. He earns Rs 6,000 a week and she earns Rs 4,000. Together, they support three children and their elderly parents. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. "I was happy to get an opportunity to return to agriculture, while my wife could contribute to food processing," Ramar says. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further . He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, maintenance, plumbing and electrical repairs. Today he manages much of the daily farm work and coordinates packing and dispatch. His wife, Sumithra, stitches cotton tea bags from home using a machine supplied by Kalaiselvi. When a customer complained that a tea bag floated instead of staying immersed, Sasikumar suggested adding two stitches. The adjustment worked and became part of the process. "I never imagined that a job I started as a helper would allow me to learn so many skills and take on such responsibilities," he says. "I feel that my experience matters and that I can contribute ideas that make a real difference to the business." A longer life for the fruit, and a new beginning after 40 Kalaiselvi estimates that nearly 60 percent of suitable surplus produce that might previously have gone unused is now processed. It is an approximate, seasonal figure, rather than a fixed share of everything the farm grows. Processing also means the family has more ways to earn from fruit instead of relying only on fresh-produce prices during a short harvest window. By December 2024, Aruvi had reached more than 4,000 customers and recorded around 450 orders in one month. Sales have come through its website, Amazon and WhatsApp, while exhibitions, farmers' markets and food events have helped people across India discover the products. Some ingredients are sourced from neighbouring producers, giving the business opportunities to connect with other growers too. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. Growth comes with its own demands. Availability changes with each season, small batches take planning, and products without synthetic preservatives need careful hygiene and moisture control. Kalaiselvi has had to learn about equipment, investment, pricing and winning customer trust. "Perhaps the biggest challenge was changing our own mindset. From thinking like farmers who wanted to avoid wastage to thinking like entrepreneurs who had to create a product, a brand, and a market around that surplus," she says. She hopes to improve processing capacity and quality checks, work with more local farmers, reach retailers and business customers, and create more jobs. But she keeps returning to the person who made the journey possible: her father, who began tending the ancestral land long before she imagined working on it herself. "Today, the farm means much more to me than a piece of ancestral land. It is a part of my family's history, a teacher, a workplace, and the foundation of Aruvi Eco," she says. She was over 40 when she began learning food processing. Starting again meant being a beginner after years in an established career, a possibility she hopes other women will consider too. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. "I started this journey in a completely new field after 40, and there were many things I had to learn from scratch," she says. "That experience has given me a strong belief that women, and anyone who feels it is 'too late' to begin something new, should not let age stop them." What began as a question about unsold amla has become a way to carry forward her father's work, give the harvest more time to find a buyer and build livelihoods around the farm she once visited on holidays. All pictures courtesy Kalaiselvi.

items.title: Η ανακάλυψη του Αλτσχάιμερ αποκαλύπτει ένα κρυφό ελάττωμα στο σύστημα καθαρισμού του εγκεφάλου
items.titleOriginal: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες εντόπισαν ένα γονίδιο που βοηθά τα κύτταρα του ανοσοποιητικού συστήματος του εγκεφάλου να περιέχουν επιβλαβείς πλάκες που συνδέονται με τη νόσο του Αλτσχάιμερ, αποκαλύπτοντας πιθανώς έναν νέο τρόπο καταπολέμησης της νόσου. Όταν το γονίδιο δυσλειτουργούσε στα ποντίκια, η τοξική συσσώρευση επιταχύνθηκε και οι γνωστικές ικανότητες μειώθηκαν, δημιουργώντας ελπίδες ότι η αποκατάσταση της λειτουργίας του θα μπορούσε να βοηθήσει στην προστασία του εγκεφάλου.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

items.descriptionOriginal: A family in Los Angeles’ Lake Balboa neighborhood has a holiday tradition that dates back about 80 years. Every Thanksgiving, the host and a helper write “Turkey Notes” for all the loved ones attending the feast. The only rule? Include the word “turkey” somewhere in the text. The notes range from silly rhymes (“Turkey red, turkey yellow, turkey says you’re an awesome fellow”) to sincere celebrations of guests’ recent accomplishments. The writers then wrap the notes in colorful tissue paper and “roll them like a Tootsie Roll with ribbon on each end,” Nice News reader Sadie shared, adding that the ritual makes for some of her favorite memories. Sadie is one of the dozens of readers who answered our call earlier this month to submit the seasonal family traditions they partake in. Multiple made us laugh out loud, while others were deeply touching. We rounded up a selection for you to peruse — and they just might inspire new shared activities for your own holiday gatherings. Iuliia Anisimova—iStock/Getty Images Plus The hood ornament from my husband’s mother’s car he wrecked as a teenager. It was his only Christmas gift that year. It’s the first ornament we hang every year. – Katherine (Lake Wylie, South Carolina) Thanksgiving Eve, we have a family/friend gathering called BAGG, which stands for Bucket-A-Go-Go. We started this tradition because my husband was tired of eating turkey on Thanksgiving and wanted a change. Nobody wanted to change the Thanksgiving menu, so BAGG was created! Every family brings their own meal but the No. 1 rule is that it must NOT be turkey! The tradition started with a bucket of chicken but now it is whatever the family brings (but NO turkey). One year someone brought a turkey sandwich and they were booed! – Lauren (Roanoke, Virginia) Cookies! We have a cookie trade! Everyone bakes two to three different types of cookies and then we get together for a Christmas party and eat cookies while spending time together. At the end of the get-together, we all split up the cookies so everyone gets to take home a few of each type of cookie. – Stacy (La Mesa, California) My three children were young when their dad and I divorced. He lived in a different state and this meant the children were always torn between celebrating Thanksgiving and Christmas with either mom or dad. So the children and I invited our exclusive holiday — Thanksmas — which was celebrated in early December. We decorated with both fall and Christmas decorations, cooked a meal of Thanksgiving and Christmas dishes, and enjoyed holiday music. And they never had to decide between celebrating Thanksmas with mom or dad each year — it was ours, and ours alone! – Norine (Winchester, Virginia) In our family, we write funny clues on the gifts. While opening them, we read the clues aloud and try to guess what the gift is. – Jennifer (Duluth, Minnesota) My brother sent me an orange tree the year our dad died. Purple and orange were his favorite colors, so I decorated it with purple ornaments. It now goes up in October and transitions from a Halloween tree with bats to a Thanksgiving tree with turkey hands made by my 10 grandchildren, and then to the Christmas tree. Reminders of both my dad and my thoughtful brother. – Debra (Olathe, Kansas) I love putting out my holiday decorations from my favorite holidays, Diwali and Thanksgiving to Christmas. I also celebrate my decorations every year inside my house trying new styles as I desire after talking with my household for what we all like most. – Sautam (Massachusetts) Every year my husband and I host “Nacho Christmas.” It came about because we both wanted a chill holiday with plenty of quality time with any friends and family that want to stop through. We set up the nacho bar so people can eat whenever they come by — no need to coordinate a meal at a set time. … It’s such a huge hit that a friend had a terrible nightmare where I told her she can’t come anymore and she woke up crying. Nacho Christmas for the win. – Wendy (Chicago, Illinois) My son and I watch a holiday movie every night, beginning with Miracle on 34th Street on Thanksgiving Eve. We will have the tree up and lit as well, and then add a few ornaments every day. We always save a few so friends and family can hang something when they come over. Of course we go to see the tree at Rockefeller Center and the Rockettes every year as well! – Peggy (New York City) Making Aebleskivers, a Danish round ball pancake, on Christmas morning. They are the size of a golf ball and you make them in a pan with round holes. When the bottom of the pancake is cooked, you turn it over to cook the top side using a knitting needle. When done they can be eaten as is or with powdered sugar or honey, or you can split them open and add jam, whipped cream, or pudding in the middle. It has been a family tradition for 100 years. – Kathy (Texas) Butterscotch Schnapps milkshakes. Ice cream, milk, and Schnapps. That’s it. Sit around, talk, and drink. It’s fantastic. – Emery (Saskatchewan, Canada) My family (me, my husband Tim, and our two sons: TJ, 22, and Joey, 18) saves all the holiday cards we receive throughout the season and open them all at once after dessert on Christmas Eve. We started this tradition about 10 years ago and it’s been a favorite of everyone’s. This way, Tim and I can share who our nonlocal friends are, but over time, our sons know them and recognize them, even if they’ve never met them in person. And it’s a good way for someone not to miss some important updates. We just wish more friends and families still sent out cards. We love them. – Amy (Poulsbo, Washington) Every year for Hanukkah when my kids were still at home, we made latkes, played games, lit candles, and invited friends over. Some years, instead of giving individual gifts, we did one big family experience together. When the kids were in their teens, we decided that the first of the eight nights would be dedicated to charity, so instead of exchanging presents, we bought them for others in need or made a donation. – Elaine (Baltimore, Maryland) While raising our children in New Hampshire, we had many winter days where we lost electricity because of ice/snow storms. When the kids were very young, we lost electricity one Christmas Eve. But having a wood stove as the primary way to heat the house, at least we were warm. So, for lighting, we placed lit candles in every room and cooked some basic foods on top of the wood stove. It was magical for the children. This started a tradition on every Christmas Eve of turning off all the lights in the house, lighting only candles, and eating just hors d’oeuvres — which we have now done for 30-plus years. – Jim (North Carolina) Every Christmas, I plan a solo trip that I look forward to all year. I try to fly on Christmas Day and bring a little gift (usually a box of chocolates) for the flight attendants. While flying on the holiday tends to be a little less expensive, the real benefit is that people are kinder and more patient with one another. It reminds me of the airport scene at the beginning of Love Actually . – Marie (Frankfurt) My father is a Methodist minister. When he was in seminary shortly after World War II, he attended a Christmas party. A warm punch was served and he really liked it. He obtained the recipe and we’ve made the wassail punch every year since! We still have the original typed recipe on crinkly typewriter paper. – Carol (Alameda, California) Fruitcakes. Every Halloween weekend, I make fruitcakes with raisins, currants, apricots, pecans, cinnamon, clove, mace, and, yes, some of the traditional citron but less. Sherry and brandy poured over them every weekend until the weeks between Thanksgiving and Christmas. My paternal grandmother kept them in her pantry and I loved to watch her take them out, unwrap the wax paper, and pour sherry through cheesecloth then re-wrap and set on the self. She is with me all the time I make these. – Susan Conklin (Hood River, Oregon) My two sons are grown now, but when they were small they would make an ornament for the tree. The early ones were simple, a scrap of fabric (I had to sew the seams as they were only 2 and 4 years old), stuffed little pillows with fluffy cotton. As the years went by, the ornaments became quite amazing for little hands. As a 4-year-old, my youngest was able to complete a framed cross stitch on his own. This was a tradition until they each left for college. I now hang about 30 wildly creative ornaments on my own tree. – Ki’ihele (Hawai’i) Making gifts for my family and my friends, be it knitted mittens, a painting, or special desserts, while I enjoy the winter scenery outside my kitchen window. – Dianne (River Falls, Wisconsin) About a decade ago, I began a tradition with my son (now 13) that we call the thankful tree. I found a little decorative tree and we have leaf-shaped papers with string. Every night of November, we each write down something we are grateful for from that day, share them out loud, and hang them on the tree. By the end of the month, our tree (and hearts) are bursting with gratitude, and I save and label the “leaves” from each year, so we can look back on memories and gratitude. – Sarah (Denver, Colorado) I am one of 10 children. When we were born, my mother knit us a Christmas stocking with our names on it. As we married and had children, she knit stockings for our spouses and her grandchildren. My brother-in-law built a faux fireplace that we keep at the Elks Club. We get together every Christmas Eve and hang our stockings! There are usually 40-50 stockings! – Mary (Warren, New Jersey) Every December, we delight in attending a carol service at a huge old church on Bloor St. — a main street in the downtown. People put twenties on the collection plate which goes entirely to support the Toronto Star Santa Claus Fund begun by newspaper editor Joe Atkinson so underprivileged children would receive a Christmas gift. Boxes contain mitts, warm hats, books, candy, etc. This was especially welcomed during the Great Depression and continues the spirit of giving to this day! – Gail (Toronto, Canada) Since college, my sibling and I have played Santa for our parents. It’s our way of giving back. Yes, our parents still play Santa for us, and Santa gifts are, dare I say, now more anticipated than family gifts. – Eli (Seattle, Washington) Every year, we rent a big house or conference center for around 20 family members. We bring a Ping-Pong table if need be and we play card games, board games, puzzles, and, of course, Ping-Pong. Wednesday night is cheese streak night. On Thursday, we all work to make the Thanksgiving meal. Friday we hike and play, play, play. It never gets old. This year we are trying a new location, the Jersey Shore. – Joyce (Ottsville, Pennsylvania) My grandmother’s favorite color was purple; she passed about 20 years ago. Each year for Christmas, my mom and I wrap a special package in purple paper to give to each other from my grandmom, Mabelle. – Kimberleigh (Maryland) RELATED: We Asked Readers to Share the Best Compliments They’ve Received

items.descriptionOriginal: Abandoned with two young children in a foreign country, she had every reason to give up. But she chose to begin again. ❤️ After an abusive marriage, physical assault and abandonment, she found herself raising two children alone while battling depression and trying to rebuild her life from scratch. But she refused to let her circumstances define her future. She started working as a freelance makeup artist, gradually built her own beauty business and returned to university in 2024. For three years, she balanced motherhood, work and education, making sacrifices that often meant missing precious moments with her children. And then came the moment that made it all worthwhile. As she walked across the convocation stage, her children cheered: “That's my mom!” 🥹 Today, she is a university graduate, a beauty entrepreneur and a mother showing her children the power of courage, resilience and perseverance. Her journey is a reminder that starting over is never easy, but it's never too late to reclaim your dreams. Because some victories are bigger than a degree. This one was hers. ❤️ What does her journey teach you about never giving up? #SingleMother #SingleMothers #WomenEmpowerment #DomesticAbuseSurvivor #WomenEntrepreneurs #Motherhood #InspirationalStories #WomenWhoInspire #NeverGiveUp #Resilience #BeautyEntrepreneur #EducationMatters #SurvivorStories #MotherhoodJourney #TheBetterIndia

items.descriptionOriginal: India's most extraordinary landscapes do not always announce themselves with grand monuments or marked tourist trails. Some are hidden beneath tropical forests, others rise out of the sea, and a few preserve evidence of geological events that unfolded millions of years ago. Now, several of these remarkable places are attracting international attention. India's UNESCO Tentative List has expanded in 2026, with two particularly fascinating natural heritage additions in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands: the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang and the Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, comprising Barren and Narcondam islands. These additions build on seven natural heritage properties submitted in August 2025, taking the story beyond a handful of destinations to a remarkable cross-section of India's geological history. But what makes these places special, where can travellers experience them, and what should visitors know before setting out? More importantly, how can we explore them without damaging the very landscapes that make them extraordinary? A landscape shaped by two kinds of volcanoes The first of the two new natural properties is the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang, on Great Andaman Island, about 100 km north of Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair). Baratang's Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex, Andaman and Nicobar Islands: Beneath Baratang's tropical canopy, ancient limestone caves and bubbling mud volcanoes reveal Earth's restless underground world. Photograph: ( Nicobar Times ) Picture a forested island where the ground opens into limestone caves, narrow fissures, and underground chambers. Over millions of years, marine organisms, including shells and corals, accumulated and compacted to form the limestone. Rainwater gradually dissolved parts of this rock, creating the intricate cave systems found here. But the island has another geological surprise. Its mud volcanoes, locally called Jalki , release slurries of mud, water, and gases rather than molten rock. Unlike conventional volcanoes, these formations do not erupt magma. They are driven by pressure and movement within underground sediment layers. After remaining dormant for around 20 years, Baratang's mud volcanoes became active again in 2025. The Geological Survey of India identified the mud volcano as a Geo-Heritage Site that year. The caves also support specialised subterranean ecosystems, making their conservation important beyond their geological appeal. The second property, Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, brings together Barren Island and Narcondam Island. Both emerged from the tectonic processes associated with the Indian Plate moving beneath the Burma microplate. Barren Island, approximately 138 km northeast of Sri Vijaya Puram, is South Asia's only active volcano. Its first recorded eruption dates to 1787. More recently, it recorded mild eruptions in September 2025, followed by an ash plume rising approximately 1.2 km in January 2026. Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, Narcondam Island: Cloaked in dense forests, Narcondam shelters rare wildlife, including its remarkable endemic hornbill, far from bustling tourist trails. Photograph: ( Andaman Ferry Ticket ) Narcondam, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Its densely forested volcanic landscape rises 710 metres above sea level and supports species found nowhere else, including the Narcondam hornbill. Unlike Barren Island, which is known for its surrounding marine environment, Narcondam is not open to tourism. Access is restricted, and visitors should not attempt independent trips or landings. These islands are important precisely because their ecosystems remain relatively undisturbed. A UNESCO listing should not be mistaken for an invitation to explore every part of them. Seven more landscapes that tell India's geological story The two Andaman additions join seven natural properties submitted to UNESCO in August 2025. Together, they reveal just how varied India's geological heritage is. In Maharashtra, the Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar preserve evidence of enormous volcanic eruptions around 66 million years ago. Their successive lava flows created the distinctive stepped rock formations of the region. Visitors should stick to established viewpoints and avoid disturbing exposed geological formations. Deccan Traps, Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, Maharashtra: Layer upon layer of ancient lava tells the story of volcanic eruptions that reshaped India's western landscape. Photograph: ( IUGS ) Off Karnataka's Malpe coast, the St Mary's Island Cluster is famous for its unusual columnar basalt formations. These polygonal rock structures developed as molten lava cooled and contracted approximately 85 million years ago. The islands are accessible by ferry, subject to seasonal conditions. Resist the temptation to collect rock fragments or climb fragile formations. Meghalaya's Meghalayan Age Caves include Mawmluh, Mawsmai, Arwah and Krem Puri. Mawmluh Cave is particularly significant because a mineral deposit found there helped establish the Meghalayan Age, the youngest stage of the Holocene geological epoch. Cave formations take thousands of years to develop, so visitors should never touch, scratch or break them. Explore with authorised guides. Nagaland's Naga Hill Ophiolite in Kiphire district offers a glimpse into the Earth's ancient oceanic crust and upper mantle. Ophiolites are fragments of ocean floor pushed onto land through tectonic activity. The landscape also has ecological significance, making local guidance and respect for wildlife essential. In Andhra Pradesh, Erra Matti Dibbalu, or the Red Sand Hills, near Visakhapatnam, displays striking red and brown sedimentary formations. Wind and water erosion have shaped these hills over time, preserving evidence of changing environmental and climatic conditions. Visitors should avoid walking over unstable formations or leaving waste behind. Further south, the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills includes the Eparchaean Unconformity and the Silathoranam natural rock arch. The latter is particularly fascinating: its formation represents an exceptionally old geological history, with the rocks in the region recording more than a billion years of Earth's past. The surrounding hills also carry religious significance, so visitors must respect temple and forest regulations. Varkala Cliffs, Kerala: Sedimentary layers meet the Arabian Sea at Varkala, where dramatic cliffs reveal millions of years of geological history. Photograph: ( Travelladda ) Finally, Kerala's Varkala Cliffs expose layers of the Warkalli Formation, dating to the Mio-Pliocene period. Their striking sedimentary bands overlook the Arabian Sea, while natural springs add to their geological importance. However, the cliffs face pressure from increasing tourism and construction. Visitors should keep away from unstable edges and follow safety instructions. The responsibility that comes with discovery A place becoming popular can bring income to nearby communities, but it can also put pressure on fragile ecosystems. The challenge is to ensure that tourism does not destroy what makes these destinations worth visiting. Before travelling, check local entry permissions, seasonal restrictions, and forest department guidelines. Some locations, particularly caves and protected islands, have restricted access. Never assume that a place being on UNESCO's Tentative List means it is open to unrestricted tourism. India's natural wonders are more than breathtaking landscapes; they are living archives of Earth's history, deserving protection for generations. Photograph: ( Travel and Leisure Asia ) Choose local guides and community-run stays wherever possible. Carry reusable water bottles, avoid single-use plastics, and take all waste back with you. Do not collect rocks, fossils, shells or other natural material. At coastal destinations, avoid disturbing marine habitats, and at forest sites, keep noise levels low and maintain a safe distance from wildlife. There are already examples of tourism supporting conservation across India. In Nagaland's Khonoma village , community-led tourism allows visitors to experience local culture while supporting conservation efforts. Similarly, community-led travel companies are creating opportunities for travellers to contribute directly to local livelihoods. Travellers can also take inspiration from five Indian journeys that support wildlife and nature conservation and learn from sustainable travel practices that minimise waste and respect local ecosystems. India's geological heritage is not simply a collection of spectacular views. These landscapes preserve evidence of volcanic eruptions, shifting tectonic plates, ancient oceans and evolving ecosystems. Their importance extends far beyond their potential as tourist destinations. Being included on UNESCO's Tentative List is an important step towards international recognition, but it is not the finish line. The real achievement will be ensuring that these places remain intact for generations to come. After all, the best way to experience a natural wonder is to leave it just as wonderful for the next person. Sources ' Seven Natural Heritage Sites from India Added to UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage ': by Ministry of Culture for Press Information Bureau, Published on 18 September 2025. ' Sustainable Tourism: Travel with Purpose ': by Meghalaya Tourism, official tourism website, undated

Το έργο ξεκινά από μια ήσυχη στιγμή απολογισμού κατά τη διάρκεια των χρόνων της στη βιομηχανία της εξαιρετικής εστίασης, όταν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every Tuesday, Toronto chef Maddy Goldberg ties on an apron at her local food bank and transforms whatever random ingredients she finds -- onions, carrots, a forgotten bag of raw red lentils -- into 100 hot meals for families who need them. The work traces back to a quiet moment of reckoning during her years in the fine dining industry, when she finally asked herself a question more people might benefit from sitting with: "What can I actually do?" For Goldberg, the answer wasn't grand -- it was a free Tuesday and a phone call to a food bank. "I wanted to do something where the goal wasn't to make money off of it," she says. "It was just to feed people, which is why I wanted to cook in the first place." Her story is a small reminder that the gap between caring about something and actually doing something about it is often narrower than it appears.

items.description: Φανταστείτε να μπείτε σε ένα σπίτι και να βρείτε ένα ρυάκι να ρέει κάτω από τα πόδια σας. Όχι έξω από την είσοδο ή σε κήπο σχεδιασμένο να μοιάζει με φυσικό υδάτινο σώμα, αλλά ακριβώς κάτω από ένα διαφανές γυάλινο δάπεδο. Κοιτάξτε ψηλά, και υπάρχει ένα δέντρο που πλαισιώνεται από γυάλινους τοίχους και μια γυάλινη οροφή. Περπατήστε λίγο πιο πέρα, και η αρχιτεκτονική ανοίγει προς μια κοιλάδα, επιτρέπει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking into a house and finding a stream flowing beneath your feet. Not outside the entrance or in a garden designed to resemble a natural waterbody, but directly beneath a transparent glass floor. Look up, and there is a tree framed by glass walls and a glass roof. Walk a little further, and the architecture opens towards a valley, allowing the surrounding landscape to become part of the experience. This is Whispers of the Wild, a residential project by MAWI Design, led by Chennai-based architect Malli Saravanan , in Yercaud, Tamil Nadu. But the most interesting thing about this house is not what its architects added to the landscape. It is what they chose not to take away. Spread across a 10,000-square-foot plot in the eco-sensitive Shervaroy Hills, the 2,400-square-foot residence was designed for a family of six. Completed in 2024, it occupies two levels and sits within Wild Orchid, a 100-acre residential community that follows an eco-sensitive development approach. "We wanted the terrain to flow naturally over here and then bring the entire thing out," Saravanan tells The Better India . "I wanted much of it to remain tucked into the landscape, with its built form designed to sit beneath the surrounding tree canopy." The tree that became the centre of the design When the MAWI Design team first visited the property, they found a sloping site with a valley opening up on one side. A mature tree occupied a prominent position on the land, its canopy extending across the site. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. The team first conducted a total-station survey and mapped the trees across the property. This helped them understand where the existing vegetation stood and how the proposed structure could be positioned without cutting them down. "We made sure that we didn't want to cut any of the trees, and we tried to work around them without cutting the tree," Saravanan explains. The design was subsequently broken into three architectural fragments, allowing the tree to remain at the centre of the composition. "As visitors enter the house, their first visual connection is with this tree. The private and communal spaces open towards an L-shaped deck that wraps around it, creating a shared outdoor space overlooking the valley." "The tree is not retained as a decorative feature. We tried to retain this tree as the hero of the site and started building a story around this tree," he says. The same idea extends to the interiors. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement , while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. The master bedroom, meanwhile, projects outwards in a cantilevered form. Its glass frame opens towards a panoramic view of the valley. Saravanan points out that the corners have been kept free of columns to preserve the expansive views. "We don't have any TV walls and stuff, so the bedrooms are designed to open towards nature, too," he says, describing the decision to make the surrounding landscape the primary visual experience. A stream that disappeared, and an attempt to bring back its memory One of the most distinctive features of Whispers of the Wild is its entrance foyer. Here, the team separated two building blocks to create a transition space that feels open rather than enclosed. They also introduced a cascading water feature beneath a glass floor. There is a story behind this intervention. The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement, while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) "We tried to pull out the rocks that were there at the site. And then we set up a water feature so that when one comes into this foyer space, the flooring is completely glass, so the water will be flowing underneath," Saravanan says. The experience is deliberately immersive. The glass floor reveals the water below, while glass on the opposite side reflects the trees. A glass roof completes the visual connection with the surroundings. What happens during heavy rainfall? The team incorporated rainwater harvesting and constructed a storage tank to collect water from the roof and other catchment areas for use within the house. "Since it is a slope side, we have made sure that when there is heavy rain, the water gets collected and then it is harvested inside the ground, and the overflow gets down to the valley," Saravanan says. There is, however, an important distinction in the project's assessment of water systems. Saravanan confirms that the team conducted a soil test and a general site survey, but did not undertake a separate hydrological assessment . What happens when the house borrows from the landscape? The walls of the house incorporate locally available random rubble stones, many sourced from within the property or nearby areas. Saravanan explains that construction activity in and around Yercaud often brings up large boulders when soil is excavated. Some of these were already available on the property, while smaller stones were sourced from nearby community areas. "We use this material as a kind of expression of the context. We use the same material in the exterior and also in the interior, so that we create a very timeless kind of palette inside the house," he says. The rubble stone is used as an exterior-facing element over brick construction, rather than as the primary structural wall. According to Saravanan, the thickness and overall mass of the wall contribute to thermal comfort within the house. The flooring uses leathered Kota stone. Saravanan wanted the sensation of walking indoors to resemble the experience of walking outdoors. The stone's natural texture and coolness were important considerations. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) "For us, the first thing is experiential. The second is the sustainable aspect of it, and third is the aesthetics," he explains. Oxide finishes and other natural materials complete the palette. The intention was not to create a polished, artificial version of nature, but to let the materials sit comfortably within the surrounding landscape. The team also retained the site's existing vegetation, including fruit-bearing plants and a fig tree. Saravanan says they avoided introducing non-native plants. The one notable addition was bamboo, planted along the property boundary. It serves two purposes. The community has a pathway running along the edge of the property, and the bamboo provides visual privacy for the residents . It also contributes to the sensory experience of the house. "We love the rustling sounds. So whenever there is wind, you listen to the rustling sounds, and it adds to the overall experience of the space," he says. Does wildlife find a place here, too? A house in a hillside landscape cannot be understood only through its architecture. The Shervaroy Hills have their own distinctive vegetation, including shrubs and fruit-bearing plants. Saravanan says the team tried to retain the existing flora and make the new landscape blend with the region. He has also noticed changes in the presence of birds and other smaller wildlife around the property. "Butterflies, birds, and peacocks started coming after this," he says, adding that peacocks are frequently seen around the house. A home that changes how its residents experience nature Interestingly, Whispers of the Wild was not originally conceived as a permanent retirement home. The client, 67-year-old Chandrapratapan from Salem, purchased the property. "One of our favourite things about living here is never knowing what we might see in the morning. Peacocks often wander by in the garden, squirrels move between the trees, and occasionally we spot a mongoose passing through. We've started recognising different birds by their calls. The old tree is probably the busiest spot on the property, with birds and insects constantly moving through it," he shares with The Better India . "This has made us much more aware of all the life we share this place with. We love that we've been able to preserve much of what was already here — the trees, the slope and the natural landscape," Chandrapratap adds. Saravanan also believes this reflects a shift in how people think about their homes. "We are in a very rushed world, with all these tensions and pressure, running here and there. At the end of it, people want to spend time for themselves," he says. He has noticed more people looking beyond metropolitan neighbourhoods for homes that offer a connection with nature and a sense of calm. For him, this is not simply about having a second home or spending money on elaborate interiors. It is about the relationship between people, their surroundings and the communities they live in. Can building with nature also make financial sense? There is another question worth asking. Is this approach financially viable, or is it an architectural luxury accessible only to people who can afford expensive homes in the hills? Saravanan puts the construction cost of Whispers of the Wild at approximately Rs 1.3-1.4 crore. He considers this reasonable for a project of its scale and location, particularly because transporting materials to a hill station and arranging labour can increase construction costs. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) "We had all those good elements around the site. We wanted the site not to be manicured. We wanted things to be imperfect and just flow seamlessly," he says. "We don't know where that new landscape starts or where the new construction starts. It should feel like it's very well lived in, especially the exterior parts." The project does not establish that this approach is cheaper in every situation. Its costs depend on the terrain, construction requirements, materials and site conditions. But it offers an example of how existing natural features can become part of the architectural experience rather than being removed and recreated. Before building on a hillside, what should architects reconsider? For Saravanan, the first step is to understand the site before drawing up the building. "First, we need to understand the existing terrain, the flora, the fauna, and the existing site conditions. Making less impact on nature is the first fundamental thing they need to consider," he says. He believes the value of a mature tree, for instance, cannot be measured simply in terms of the money required to plant another one. "Today, we can buy anything, but a well-grown tree like this, with whatever money they want, they can't buy it." He also emphasises the importance of keeping the building footprint small. At Whispers of the Wild, the architects used cantilevered sections and elevated portions to reduce the amount of building mass touching the ground. The intention was to allow the landscape to continue around the structure. "If the footprint is very small, it is always better. It is the idea that a building does not always need to begin with a cleared, levelled piece of land," he adds. All pictures: mawidesign.india

Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν ότι μικροσκοπικά πλαστικά σωματίδια μπορούν να αλληλεπιδράσουν με το νερό για να δημιουργήσουν εξαιρετικά αντιδραστικά μόρια ικανά να βλάψουν κύτταρα και ιστούς. items.descriptionOriginal: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

items.titleOriginal: Halló! Habari! Learn How to Say Hello in 25 Different Languages
items.description: Το 1973, οι Αμερικανοί αδελφοί Μάικλ και Μπράιαν ΜακΚόρμακ έστειλαν 1.360 επιστολές σε επτά γλώσσες σε κυβερνητικούς ηγέτες σε όλο τον κόσμο, ενθαρρύνοντάς τους να συμμετάσχουν στην εναρκτήρια Παγκόσμια Ημέρα Γειας. «Θέλαμε να κάνουμε κάτι για να γιορτάσουμε τη σημασία της προσωπικής επικοινωνίας για τη διατήρηση της ειρήνης», δήλωσε ο Michael, ανώτερος υπάλληλος στο Χάρβαρντ εκείνη την εποχή, προηγ.…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 1973, American brothers Michael and Brian McCormack mailed 1,360 letters in seven languages to government leaders across the globe, encouraging them to participate in the inaugural World Hello Day. “We wanted to do something to celebrate the importance of personal communication to preserving peace,” Michael, a senior at Harvard at the time, previously told the university paper, The Crimson . He and Brian had pooled their money to pay for the postage, with the goal of getting their recipients to agree to, quite literally, spread the word. The idea behind the holiday, observed every Nov. 21, is that differences should be addressed through peaceful conversation rather than conflict. To participate, all you have to do is say “hello” to 10 people. Fifteen countries pledged their support the first year; today, individuals in 180 have joined in — including 31 Nobel Peace Prize winners who sent the brothers letters championing World Hello Day. “It’s something people can do on their own in widely different places,” Michael explained to the Associated Press back in 1991. “It gives people a chance to do something about the world; it empowers them.” Ready to get started? Before you do, consider broadening your reach by learning how to say hello in a few different languages — below are 25 translations (plus two bonus ones, just for fun). Portuguese – olá Hindi – namaste Dutch – hallo Filipino – kumusta Ukrainian – pryvit Arabic – marhaban Polish – witam Greek – geiá sou Hebrew – shalom Mandarin – nǐ hǎo Spanish – hola Esperanto – saluton Yoruba – pẹlẹ o Hawaiian – aloha Japanese – kon’nichiwa Icelandic – halló Swahili – habari French – bonjour Zulu – sawubona Korean – annyeonghaseyo Persian – salām Turkish – merhaba Swedish – hej Samoan – talofa Italian – ciao Klingon (from Star Trek ) – nuqneH Dothraki (from Game of Thrones ) – m’athchomaroon

items.title: 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές
items.titleOriginal: 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices
items.description: Happy Eco News 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 8 λεπτά 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές Η υγειονομική περίθαλψη παρήγαγε περίπου το 8,5 τοις εκατό όλων των εκπομπών αερίων του θερμοκηπίου στις ΗΠΑ το 2018, σύμφωνα με μια ανάλυση του 2020 στον τομέα Health Affairs που θέτει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Reading Time: 8 minutes 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Health care produced roughly 8.5 percent of all US greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 , according to a 2020 analysis in Health Affairs that put the sector’s total at about 553 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent. My argument here is simple: healthcare SaaS, the software a clinic rents over the internet instead of running on its own machines, is one of the cheapest ways for a practice to shrink its share of that number, and most of the savings show up in the budget too. Now picture one family clinic. Behind the front desk sits a back room lined with manila folders, a shredding bin and a fax machine that still rattles every afternoon. Across the hall, a server closet hums all night with its door propped open because the room runs hot. That clinic is not a villain. It is just carrying what I call everyday carbon : the emissions that come from paper, idle servers, car trips and supplies that expire on a shelf. None of it is dramatic. All of it adds up, and almost all of it can be trimmed without touching a single clinical decision. I have spent years building and fixing software for clinics and hospitals, from appointment tools for two-doctor practices to records systems for regional hospital groups. The five changes below are the ones I have seen stick. 1. Paperless records and e-prescribing empty the archive room Before the switch, a typical small practice runs on paper that moves. Charts travel from the shelf to the exam room and back. Prescriptions get printed, signed, handed over, and sometimes lost in a coat pocket, which means a second trip for the patient. Old files go to an off-site storage unit, and someone drives there whenever a records request comes in. After the switch, the chart lives in a cloud-based electronic health record. A prescription goes straight from the doctor’s screen to the pharmacy, so there is no paper slip and no handwriting for the pharmacist to call about. Intake forms get filled out on a phone the night before instead of on a clipboard in the waiting room. What surprised me the first time I watched a practice go through this was where the real savings hid. The paper itself mattered less than the trips around it: courier runs to the storage unit, patients coming back for a forgotten form, staff driving boxes to a shredding service. One practice I worked with turned its old archive room into a third exam room within a year, which was the moment the owner stopped calling the project “the IT thing.” Nobody misses the fax machine. (Well, one office manager did, for about a week.) 2. A slice of a big data center beats a humming server closet The on-premise server is the quiet energy hog of small health care. It runs around the clock, needs its own cooling, gets replaced every few years, and in most clinics I have visited it sits mostly idle outside office hours. Backups often mean a second machine, or a drive someone takes home on Fridays. Large cloud data centers do the same work far more efficiently, and the numbers on this are striking. A Berkeley Lab analysis published in Science found that from 2010 to 2018, global data center computing output rose 550 percent while energy use rose only 6 percent , with most of the gains coming from big operators running highly efficient facilities. When a clinic moves its records, billing and scheduling to a SaaS product, it trades a single half-used box for a tiny, well-managed slice of one of those buildings. Off-the-shelf products cover most of what a typical clinic needs, but not everything. A fertility center with an unusual lab workflow, or a rural health network that wants its own patient app tied to existing systems, often ends up working with a partner that offers healthcare software development services to build the missing piece. My advice to anyone in that position is to make the green choices at the design stage: pick a cloud region on a cleaner power grid, decide how long logs and imaging files stay in fast storage before they move to cheaper cold storage, and stop the system from keeping five copies of the same scan. Building those rules in from day one costs very little. Retrofitting them into a live system full of patient data means migrations, compliance reviews and weekend downtime, and in my experience that costs far more. One pushback comes up in nearly every conversation I have about this. Skeptics raise a fair objection: the cloud does not cut emissions, it just moves them into giant data centers, and with AI pushing demand up, those buildings are only getting hungrier. Part of that is true. AI is driving a wave of new data center construction, and it deserves close scrutiny. But a clinic is not choosing between the cloud and zero emissions. It is choosing between the cloud and a lone server in a closet with a window air conditioner, and the Berkeley Lab work shows that the efficiency gains landed at the large operators. A clinic can also ask its vendor which region hosts its data and pick one on a cleaner grid, which is a settings change, not a construction project. 3. Telehealth takes car trips off the road without anyone noticing The most visible change is also the easiest to measure. Every follow-up visit that happens over video is a round trip that never happens, and for patients in rural areas that round trip can eat half a day. A national study published in The American Journal of Managed Care in 2025 looked at claims for 44.7 million insured US adults from April to June 2023. Scaled to the whole insured adult population, the researchers estimated that telemedicine averts between 21.4 million and 47.6 million kilograms of CO2 every month , roughly the monthly emissions of 61,000 to 130,000 gasoline cars. The authors call the effect modest relative to all of health care, and they are right to. Still, that is a cut that came almost entirely from visits people preferred anyway. In the practices I have worked with, the clinics that get the most from telehealth are the ones that decide on purpose which visits belong on video. Medication check-ins, test result reviews and most mental health sessions move online well. A sprained ankle does not. There is a second, smaller commute hiding in the same change. Once records, billing and scheduling live in the cloud, the people who handle them no longer have to sit next to the server. I have seen coding and billing teams move to two office days a week, which takes a few more cars off the road and frees up desk space the clinic was paying to heat and cool. The patient keeps the afternoon. The planet keeps the gas. 4. Smarter scheduling and inventory keep vials out of the trash Waste in a clinic is rarely one big mistake. It is a slow trickle of small ones: a box of supplies ordered twice because nobody checked the cabinet, a vaccine lot that expired behind a newer one, a refrigerator that failed on Saturday night and was found on Monday morning. Before SaaS, inventory usually lives in a spreadsheet or a clipboard that one person understands. Orders go out “just in case,” because running short feels worse than overbuying. After the switch, stock levels connect to the appointment calendar, so the system knows that next week has twelve flu shot appointments and only ten doses on hand. It flags lots that are close to expiring so staff use them first, and a cheap temperature sensor in the vaccine fridge sends an alert to a phone the minute something goes wrong. I once watched a pediatric practice lose a full fridge of vaccines to a weekend power fault. After they added a connected sensor, the next fault triggered a text at 2 a.m., a staff member drove in, and the doses moved to a backup unit before any of them warmed up. Nobody wrote a sustainability report about it. It was simply less waste. Scheduling tools help in a quieter way. Automated text reminders cut no-shows, which means fewer wasted slots and fewer rebooked trips. For home health teams, route planning groups nearby visits together, so nurses drive less and see more patients in a day. The software does not care about carbon at all. It cares about minutes and miles, and the carbon follows. 5. Remote monitoring keeps patients home and out of the ambulance The last change reaches past the clinic walls. Patients with heart failure, high blood pressure or diabetes can now send daily readings from a connected scale, blood pressure cuff or glucose meter, and a nurse sees a warning sign days before it becomes an emergency. Evidence from the research side is encouraging, though not unanimous. A 2025 meta-analysis in Cureus pooled 15 studies, nine of them randomized trials, and found that remote patient monitoring reduced heart failure hospitalizations , with the strongest effect from implanted monitors and a smaller one from simpler home devices. The authors rated their confidence in the hospitalization result as moderate, which is an honest grade for a field that is still maturing. Here is where I go a step further. Every avoided hospital stay also means an ambulance ride that did not happen, a bed that did not need heating and cooling for four days, and a stack of single-use supplies that never got opened. The meta-analysis did not count any of that, so this is my own extrapolation. But anyone who has seen how much material a single admission consumes will find it hard to argue the other way. For patients, the benefit is simpler. They sleep in their own beds. What changes when a clinic makes all five moves? Put side by side, the before and after look like this. Practice Before After with SaaS Records and prescriptions Paper charts, printed scripts, fax, off-site storage runs Cloud health record, e-prescriptions sent straight to the pharmacy IT infrastructure Server closet running around the clock with its own cooling Hosted in large data centers, where Berkeley Lab found compute grew 550 percent on 6 percent more energy (2010 to 2018) Routine visits Every follow-up means a car trip Suitable follow-ups on video, an estimated 21.4 to 47.6 million kg of CO2 averted each month across insured US adults (2023 data) Supplies and scheduling Overordering, expired stock, missed fridge failures, no-shows Stock tied to the calendar, expiry alerts, fridge sensors, automated reminders Chronic care Problems surface in the emergency room Daily readings from home, fewer heart failure hospitalizations in pooled studies None of these rows asks a clinic to become a climate organization. Each one is a normal operations upgrade that happens to shrink everyday carbon along the way. Where can a clinic start this quarter? You do not need a sustainability officer to begin. Most everyday carbon sits inside decisions a practice manager already makes, so the steps below fit into budgets and meetings that exist today. Count the paper before you cut it. Spend one week tracking what gets printed, faxed, couriered or driven anywhere. The list is usually shorter than people fear and points to two or three workflows worth moving online first. Start with whatever generates car trips, because those carry the biggest footprint. Ask every software vendor where your data lives. A good SaaS provider can tell you which cloud region hosts your records and whether that region runs on a cleaner grid. If your vendor cannot answer, that tells you something about how closely they watch their own infrastructure. The same question belongs in every new contract. Make video the default for follow-ups that do not need hands. Sit down with your clinicians and agree on a short list of visit types that start as virtual unless the patient prefers otherwise. Patients in rural areas will thank you first. Review the list every six months, since comfort with video tends to grow. Connect the supply room to the calendar. Even a basic inventory module that knows upcoming appointments will stop most double orders. Add a connected temperature sensor to any fridge that holds vaccines or biologics. It is one of the cheapest insurance policies a clinic can buy. Write a retention rule for data, not just for paper. Federal and state law set how long medical records must be kept, so start there, then decide what happens to everything else: old logs, duplicate image files, test exports. Data that nobody needs still sits on powered drives somewhere, and a clear rule keeps your cloud bill and your footprint from creeping upward. A greener clinic in 2030 might look like this What follows is a picture of what is possible, not a forecast. It is a Tuesday morning in 2030. The front desk has no printer. The room that once held folders is an exam room with a window, and the old server closet stores yoga mats for the staff wellness class. Half of today’s follow-ups happen on video, so the parking lot has empty spaces. A home nurse’s route was planned overnight, with four visits on the same side of town. In the vaccine fridge, every vial is in date, because the system flagged the oldest lot last week and the team used it first. Three heart failure patients sent their morning weights before breakfast, and one of them got a phone call and a medication adjustment instead of an ambulance ride. Nothing in that scene requires a breakthrough. Every piece of it exists today. The greenest clinic of 2030 will not look heroic, just quietly well organized. The post 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices appeared first on Happy Eco News .
